name: Computer Vision
guide:
Computer vision engineering is about teaching software to extract meaning from images and video, building and tuning models that detect objects, segment scenes, track motion, or reconstruct 3D structure from 2D pixels. Day to day, that means curating and labeling visual datasets, training and evaluating convolutional and transformer-based models, and optimizing inference so a model runs fast enough for a car, a camera, or a phone. It overlaps heavily with Machine Learning Engineering, and in our data the two blur together constantly, with titles like Machine Learning Engineer, Perception or Machine Learning Engineer, Multimodal Perception and Authentication showing up under this category. The difference is focus, since a general ML engineer might work on text, tabular data, or recommendation systems, while a computer vision engineer works specifically with pixels, sensors, and spatial data. Robotics and Autonomy roles use computer vision as one input among many, alongside planning, control, and hardware integration, so a CV engineer builds the eyes while a robotics engineer builds the whole body that acts on what those eyes see.

Credentials matter more here than in many software roles. Several of the postings we pulled, including Waymo's PhD-track Machine Learning Engineer Perception LLM/VLM listing for PhD and new grad candidates and its 2027 PhD summer internship, name a graduate degree outright, and research-scientist-titled roles at the same company imply the same expectation even when unstated. A bachelor's degree in computer science, electrical engineering, or a related field opens the door at the engineer level, but a master's or PhD becomes the stronger signal as roles move toward research or staff titles. We did not see a single named certification anywhere in this sample, so if you are hoping a course completion badge will substitute for a degree or a portfolio, our data says plainly that it will not carry weight here. What does carry weight, based on the titles we tracked, is published research or a demonstrable project, since several roles are framed around specific technical problems like 3D reconstruction, SLAM, or multimodal perception rather than general coding ability.

Experience requirements track seniority closely in our sample. Entry points exist, including one junior-level Computer Vision and Machine Learning Associate role and internship or new-grad postings aimed at PhD candidates, so junior does not always mean undergraduate-only. The bulk of what we tracked sits at mid-level and senior, often built around a specific technical specialty such as continuous learning, 3D segmentation, or perception for autonomous vehicles rather than broad generalist experience. Staff and senior research scientist postings, concentrated heavily at Waymo, expect a track record of shipped or published work, not just years on a badge. Across the board, what separates candidates who get hired from those who do not appears to be a concrete body of work, a paper, a deployed model, or a project you can point to and explain, rather than a resume that simply lists years.

The tools named across our postings cluster tightly. PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX appear repeatedly as the core modeling frameworks, alongside C++ and Python as the dominant languages and CUDA for GPU-accelerated inference. Several roles explicitly list Computer Vision itself as a tagged skill, and a growing share blend it with large language model and transformer work, reflecting vision-language models as a real hiring trend rather than a buzzword. Docker, SQL, and distributed systems tools show up in a handful of postings tied to production deployment rather than research. Fine-tuning and model evaluation are named often enough to suggest that adapting existing large models, not just training from scratch, is now a standard part of the job.

We currently track approximately 18 open Computer Vision postings. Of the 34 postings in our broader working sample, only 8 carried a stated salary figure, and among those the range ran from about $113,000 to roughly $290,000 a year, though most of those numbers were single-point estimates rather than true ranges, with only one posting, from Zoox, stating an actual low-to-high band. Waymo accounts for the largest share of postings we pulled by a wide margin, followed by smaller but repeated appearances from Zoox, Scale AI, Allen Control Systems, and Caseguard. If you are targeting this field, that concentration is worth noting, since a handful of employers are doing most of the visible hiring in our data right now.
